p-kadikoy.name: Kadıköy market and the Tuesday pazar
p-kadikoy.teaser: Fish row and greengrocers five minutes up from the ferry, then the Tuesday pazar out at Hasanpaşa
p-kadikoy.story: Kadıköy's market is not a hall but a grid of short sloping streets behind Söğütlüçeşme, with Güneşlibahçe Sokağı as its spine: fishmongers at the bottom, a greengrocer at no. 9, butchers, bakers and a spice counter inside about eighty metres, and a butchers' row round the corner on Serasker Caddesi. Buy to the boats, not to a list. Commercial fishing runs 1 September to 15 April, so autumn brings palamut and lüfer, winter brings hamsi, and summer ice is mostly farmed levrek and çipura. On Tuesday the city's best-known pazar trades up at Hasanpaşa, ten minutes inland, where tomatoes go by the crate and herbs by the armful.
p-kadikoy.why: Do the street on a weekday morning, then walk inland on a Tuesday and stay for the pazar's last hour, when growers cut prices.
facts: Market streets daily; the Salı Pazarı at Hasanpaşa on Tuesday, with Friday also listed (Oct 2026)
Stalls set their own; the streets trade by day and are fullest late morning
Late morning for the fish row; the last hour before the pazar trestles come down
Whole palamut in autumn, cleaned free at the counter (say "temizlensin"); tomatoes and flat parsley at Güneşlibahçe 9; kuzu pirzola; bring bags and small notes for the pazar, which takes no cards

p-spice.name: Spice Bazaar and Hasırcılar Caddesi
p-spice.teaser: A 1660 hall built to pay for a mosque, and the back-gate street where its own traders buy
p-spice.story: Turhan Hatice Sultan, mother of Mehmed IV, had the hall built as the rent-paying arm of the New Mosque; it was going up in the last months of 1660, after that July's great fire, and its name, Mısır Çarşısı, the Egyptian market, points at the province whose revenues paid for it. Eighty-five shops remain, and spice is retreating from them in favour of boxed lokum and pistachio pyramids built for photographs. Walk the L-shaped hall for the vault, then leave by the back gate onto Hasırcılar Caddesi, where roasters, nut merchants and cheese, pickle and pulse counters sell by the kilo, for less, to people who cook.
p-spice.why: Look inside, buy outside: pul biber, nar ekşisi, walnuts and grating cheese are cheaper on Hasırcılar for the same goods.
facts: Hall daily; many Hasırcılar counters close on Sunday
Hall Mon–Sat 08:00–19:00, Sun 09:30–19:00 (OpenStreetMap, seen Aug 2026); street counters shut by early evening
A weekday morning, while the handcarts are still moving
Urfa isot, Antep pul biber, sumac and dried mint you can smell first; ask for "yarım kilo" or "çeyrek"; refuse anything pre-boxed and never accept the first saffron price

p-kadinlar.name: Kadınlar Pazarı
p-kadinlar.teaser: Siirt cheese, isot and comb honey under the Valens Aqueduct, still trading after the bazaars close
p-kadinlar.story: Below the arches of the Valens Aqueduct at Zeyrek, the streets were settled by families from Siirt and the south-east, and this market stocks what their kitchen needs: otlu peynir threaded with wild herbs, fat pistachios, isot, comb honey and dried pulses. Between the shops, büryan ovens are cut into the floor with lamb hanging in the pit; Siirt Şeref Büryan, which has its own table card, is the address for that. The hours are the surprise. OpenStreetMap has the shops working to 22:00 most days and 23:00 on Sunday, which makes this the one provisioning stop on the historic peninsula still lit when the bazaar quarters have shut.
p-kadinlar.why: Taste the otlu peynir before you buy: the herb should read as wild garlic and thyme, not salt with a green fleck.
facts: Mon–Tue 09:00–22:00; Wed–Sat 08:00–22:00; Sun 08:00–23:00 (OpenStreetMap, seen Aug 2026); shops vary
Early evening, after the Spice Bazaar has closed, uphill from it
Otlu peynir by the piece, Siirt pistachios, isot and a slab of comb honey

p-besiktas-fish.name: Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı
p-besiktas-fish.teaser: The nearest serious fish counter to a Bosphorus berth, and no ferry ride with a cold box
p-besiktas-fish.story: Beşiktaş keeps its fish trade in the covered block behind the square, two minutes from the ferry, and unlike the Beyoğlu row it is still a market before it is a restaurant: whole fish on ice, chalked per kilo, gutted and scaled at the counter for nothing. Nut counters, helva makers and greengrocers close the list within a hundred metres. Learn the lüfer ladder before you point: çinekop, sarıkanat, lüfer and kofana are one fish at four ages, and Turkey sets a minimum landing size, so a stall pushing the smallest grade is telling you about itself. On Saturday a street pazar sets up north-west of the square.
p-besiktas-fish.why: Provision fish on the European shore without crossing the water: go mid-morning and say whether you want it scaled.
facts: Fish block: hours not published, trades by day; street pazar: Saturday
Mid-morning, the busiest and freshest hour
The four lüfer grades by name; helva, nuts and dried fruit in the çarşı around the fish

p-resat.name: Reşat Balık
p-resat.teaser: A fishmonger in the Beyoğlu Balık Pazarı since 1941, still cutting fish on a Sunday afternoon
p-resat.story: The house dates itself to 1941 and still runs its counter at Sahne Sokak 8, inside the Balık Pazarı off İstiklal, with a second one out at Bostancı on Bağdat Caddesi. Be clear about the setting: the old Beyoğlu fish market around it has thinned into meyhane tables and souvenir stalls, so the row is now more restaurant than market, and the counter is the only reason to walk in. What sets Reşat apart is the clock. OpenStreetMap has it open until 19:00 on Sunday, when most Istanbul fishmongers are done by lunch, and it is the closest serious fish counter to Pera and Galata.
p-resat.why: Your Sunday fish: the one counter near Galata still cutting after lunch, cleaned while you wait.
facts: Sunday afternoon, when everything else is shut
Whatever the season has landed, cleaned at the counter; the Bostancı shop, Bağdat Caddesi No: 476/c, on the Asian side
p-resat.maps_query: Reşat Balık Sahne Sokak Beyoğlu Istanbul

p-ferikoy.name: Feriköy %100 Ekolojik Pazar
p-ferikoy.teaser: The Saturday growers' market where the residue results sit on a desk you can walk up to and read
p-ferikoy.story: Turkey's first ecological market opened on the Feriköy ground in June 2006, organised by the Buğday association, and by its fifteenth birthday it had grown to 330 stalls and 83 vendors. The model is a halk pazarı, growers selling direct, and certification rests on field visits and laboratory analyses. The thing to see is the public-relations stall, where inspection reports and residue results for what is on sale can be read on the spot. It was also the first market in the country to do away with plastic bags. The same covered yard hosts the Sunday antiques market, so check which day you have walked into.
p-ferikoy.why: Buy what city shops handle worst: raw honey, farm eggs, small-dairy butter and cheese, cold-pressed oils, unsprayed leaves.
facts: Saturday (Time Out; operator listing, seen Aug 2026)
The analiz raporu: straight stallholders send you to the results desk; honey, eggs and greens rather than staples, which are cheaper at a semt pazarı

p-kurukahveci.name: Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi
p-kurukahveci.teaser: Coffee ground to order on Tahmis Sokak since 1871, handed over warm to a queue that never stops
p-kurukahveci.story: The house is in its 155th year and runs the anniversary as "155. YIL", and its counter is still at Tahmis Sokağı 66, at the corner of the Spice Bazaar, in the purpose-built block the company credits to the architect Zühtü Başar. It keeps only three shops of its own in the city: Eminönü, a Sirkeci branch, and Söğütlüçeşme Caddesi 12 in Kadıköy. Everywhere else it is packaging. The queue is long and fast, and almost everyone in it buys one thing: Türk kahvesi, milled to order and passed over the counter still warm in its paper pack.
p-kurukahveci.why: Buy the smallest pack you will finish in a fortnight; it is ground cezve-fine and will choke an espresso basket.
facts: 08:00–20:00 per Time Out (Oct 2026, listing undated); the company publishes none, so confirm
Morning, before the bazaar crowd arrives
Türk kahvesi ground at the counter; the Kadıköy branch at Söğütlüçeşme Caddesi 12 if you are on the Asian side

p-namli.name: Namlı Gurme and the pastırma counter
p-namli.teaser: Pastırma cut thin enough to read through, at a Karaköy counter open every day from 07:00
p-namli.story: Pastırma comes from bastırma, to press: beef dried hard under çemen, a crust of crushed fenugreek, cumin, garlic and hot paprika, with Kayseri its centre since at least an 1893 British Foreign Office report. English took the word, as pastrami, by way of Yiddish. At Namlı's Karaköy counter it is sliced to order in front of you; ask for çemeni sıyrılmış, the crust scraped back, if you want the meat rather than the spice. The same counter carries kangal sucuk from the house workshop, Gelibolu and Kars eski kaşar, Erzincan tulum, Ayvalık olives, Makaron oil, tahin and Hakkari comb honey.
p-namli.why: One stop fills the cold store: vacuum-packed pastırma and sucuk keep for weeks chilled, and the counter never takes a day off.
facts: Before 10:00, when the counter is calm and cutting fresh
Çemeni sıyrılmış pastırma ₺5,400/kg; an 850 g kangal sucuk ₺1,836, bought whole; Gelibolu eski kaşar ₺1,690/kg for grating; Erzincan tulum ₺1,180/kg (online store, seen Aug 2026)

f-lale.name: Lale İşkembecisi
f-lale.teaser: Tripe soup against the last rakı, ladled at any hour on Tarlabaşı Bulvarı since 1960
f-lale.story: When the meyhane lights go off, the Beyoğlu night ends here with a bowl of işkembe dressed at the table with garlic vinegar and lemon. It does not shut: the house claims 24 hours, seven days a week.
facts: İşkembe çorbası, or tuzlama, the richer cut the regulars take
Any hour; the house claims 24 hours, 7 days (seen Aug 2026)
No, walk in; before a 04:00 crossing of the city, phone +90 212 252 69 69

f-kizilkayalar.name: Kızılkayalar
f-kizilkayalar.teaser: The ıslak burger sweating in its steam case on the Taksim corner: the city's agreed last bite
f-kizilkayalar.story: At 03:00 on the Sıraselviler corner of Taksim the steam case is still glowing, and the ıslak hamburger, small, garlicky and soaked in tomato sauce, is how the city ends a night. It publishes no closing hour; the after-midnight queue is the institution.
facts: Two ıslak hamburgers at once, and an ayran
No, it is a büfe window on the square
Büfe prices, paid at the counter

f-gulluoglu.name: Karaköy Güllüoğlu and the Güllü split
f-gulluoglu.teaser: Pistachio baklava from the one Karaköy shop, still cutting trays after the bars go quiet
f-gulluoglu.story: Baklava reached Gaziantep in 1871 with Çelebi Güllü, who had learned it from a chef in Damascus, and in 2013 Antep Baklavası became the first Turkish product to win an EU protected geographical indication. The family grew and divided. Nadir Güllü, fifth generation, runs the single Karaköy shop at Kemankeş Caddesi 67, and the house dates itself to 1843. The largest holder of the name, Faruk Güllü, has dropped Güllüoğlu from its signs and trades through many branches from a Büyükçekmece plant. Read the first name, not the surname: a Güllüoğlu counter in a mall or an airport is neither of the two.
f-gulluoglu.why: Order fıstıklı kuru by weight: the dry pistachio cut, no cream, is the one that survives the walk back to the boat.
facts: Kemankeş Caddesi No: 67, Karaköy; the only shop
Fıstıklı kuru baklava by the porsiyon or the half kilo, not by the piece

Closing time: OpenStreetMap and a travel listing say 01:00, a guide reviewed May 2026 says 23:00, so phone +90 850 308 45 45 before a late walk. Baklava itself is claimed by Byzantine, Central Asian and Arab lineages; the one Ottoman fact is the trays sent to the Janissaries on the fifteenth of Ramadan

f-haci-bekir.name: Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir
f-haci-bekir.teaser: Lokum cut from the tray at the city's oldest sugar counter, and an invention claim nobody can prove
f-haci-bekir.story: By the house's account the founder came down from Kastamonu and opened at Bahçekapı in 1777; three generations served as Şekerci Başı, head confectioner to the palace, and five have kept the shop, which grew to 88 square metres by swallowing the spice shop next door. Lokum itself is a gel of starch and sugar scented with rosewater, mastic, bergamot or lemon. Hacı Bekir is often credited with inventing it, but the Oxford Companion to Food says there is no real evidence, and Persian starch-and-sugar recipes are centuries older. Walk past the lokum to the second counter: akide şekeri, the hard palace candy the house made first.
f-haci-bekir.why: Ask for sakızlı and gül cut from the tray, never a sealed box.
facts: Hamidiye Caddesi, Bahçekapı, Fatih; branches at İstiklal Caddesi 83 and Muvakkıthane Caddesi 14-16, Kadıköy
İstiklal branch daily 08:00–21:00 (OpenStreetMap, seen Aug 2026); the house publishes no hours
Sakızlı and gül lokum by weight, fıstıklı for pistachio; akide şekeri, helva, badem ezmesi
The house is credited with inventing lokum; the Oxford Companion to Food finds no real evidence, and confectionery founding dates are often commercial rather than historical

f-saray.name: Saray Muhallebicisi
f-saray.teaser: Chicken in the milk pudding and a scorched pan bottom: what a muhallebici makes and a patisserie cannot
f-saray.story: Hüseyin Topbaş opened in Kasımpaşa in 1935 with an aim the company still prints: to feed the elegant ladies and gentlemen of Beyoğlu the finest desserts. It took until 1949 to move onto İstiklal, and that room is the one with the history; the other branches, 21 by the house's own count, are the chain it paid for. Order what the trade exists for. Tavuk göğsü is milk pudding thickened with chicken breast pounded to threads until you cannot find it; kazandibi is the same pudding scorched on the pan bottom and turned out caramel side up. At breakfast, bal kaymak with fresh bread heads the house's own list.
f-saray.why: Order tavuk göğsü once, so you can say you ate chicken for dessert and never noticed.
facts: İstiklal Caddesi, Beyoğlu (Time Out gives No. 173)
Daily 06:00–02:00 per Time Out (Oct 2026, listing undated); the house publishes none
Tavuk göğsü and kazandibi; bal kaymak with bread in the morning

f-vefa.name: Vefa Bozacısı
f-vefa.teaser: Thick, pale, faintly sour boza, poured at one Vefa counter since September 1876
f-vefa.story: Hacı Sadık Bey came from Prizren in 1870 and spent six winters carrying boza through the streets in copper vessels before opening here in September 1876, in what the house calls the first registered boza shop in the world. He fixed the style the city still expects: thick-bodied, pale yellow, caught as the fermentation bubbles first rise, only lightly sour. His son İsmail Hakkı followed him, the fourth generation runs it now, and vinegars, grape şıra and şerbet carry the shop through summer. Drink it standing, dusted with cinnamon, roasted leblebi to chew alongside, near the glass said to have been used by Atatürk.
f-vefa.why: Come between October and April, when boza is what the shop is for; in August you are buying vinegar.
facts: Daily 08:00–22:00 (OpenStreetMap, seen Aug 2026); the house publishes no hours
One glass of boza with cinnamon and leblebi
A fraction of a coffee; no price published
f-vefa.maps_query: Vefa Bozacısı Vefa Caddesi Fatih Istanbul

f-kunefe.name: Hatay Medeniyetler Sofrası
f-kunefe.teaser: Antakya künefe from the copper dish, eaten in the minute while the cheese still pulls
f-kunefe.story: The house came north from Hatay, and the reason to end a meal here is the region's dessert: shredded kadayıf packed round fresh, unsalted, unaged cheese, baked in a shallow copper dish until both faces are dark, then drowned in syrup at the pass. It is only itself while the cheese still pulls, and it dies within minutes of leaving the copper, so order it at the end and eat it the moment it lands. The İstiklal room faces the French Consulate, but OpenStreetMap puts the door just behind the avenue on Meşelik Sokağı, so expect to turn the corner. A second room is out at Etiler.
f-kunefe.why: One künefe shared after a full Hatay table is plenty; never take it away.
facts: İstiklal Caddesi No: 39, opposite the French Consulate; also Nispetiye Caddesi No: 18, Etiler
Künefe, at the end of the meal

f-mado.name: Mado and kesme dondurma
f-mado.teaser: Kahramanmaraş ice cream stiff enough for knife and fork, at any decent branch
f-mado.story: The company traces it to snow carried down from Ahır Dağı above Kahramanmaraş and enriched with milk, honey and salep. Yaşar Kanbur began by selling ice cream from a small shop beside the Aras bus garage; the family built a Kahramanmaraş factory in 1965, brought in machines in 1970 and modernised properly in 1989. Two ingredients do the work: goat milk, from the company's own farm, and salep, the ground orchid tuber that makes the ice cream stretch and refuse to melt. Demand has thinned the region's wild orchids enough that Turkey banned salep export. With several hundred branches, it is a reference point, not a pilgrimage.
f-mado.why: Ask for kesme dondurma sade, the plain slab, so goat milk and salep are the whole flavour; the cone is the tourist version.
facts: Branches across the city; no flagship verified
Kesme dondurma, sade, eaten with knife and fork

f-baylan.name: Baylan Pastanesi
f-baylan.teaser: The republic's oldest pâtisserie, and the ice-cream coupe Harry Lenas invented there in 1954
f-baylan.story: Filip Lenas, a Greek of Albanian origin, opened in 1923 with his cousin Yorgi Kiriçi in Deva Çıkmazı, as Loryan, the Turkish ear's version of Le Orient, and moved onto İstiklal in 1928. The Kadıköy shop most people now mean by Baylan was opened by Mikail Lenas in 1961. Its own invention is the Kup Griye, created by Harry Lenas in 1954: vanilla and caramel ice cream under whipped cream, honeyed almonds and caramel sauce, a kedidili biscuit on the side. Altınmarka, owner of Kahve Dünyası, bought the business in 2009 and has kept opening rooms, at Galataport in 2021 and Kız Kulesi in 2024.
f-baylan.why: Take a table at the Kadıköy shop and order the Kup Griye by name; it is the one thing you cannot get anywhere else.
facts: Hacı Bekir's Kadıköy counter, four doors along the same street
f-baylan.maps_query: Baylan Pastanesi Muvakkıthane Caddesi Kadıköy Istanbul

v-yemek.name: Yemek ve Kültür
v-yemek.teaser: The scholarly food journal that grew out of a Kadıköy kebab shop, four issues a year in print only
v-yemek.story: The first issue appeared in January 2005 from Çiya, the house behind Çiya Sofrası, and it has come out four times a year since, in print only. Zeynep Dağdeviren is the responsible editor and Musa Dağdeviren sits on the board, filing seven forgotten folk recipes in every issue. The advisory board includes Evangelia Balta, the historian of the Turkish-speaking Ottoman Orthodox Christians, which tells you how seriously the journal takes the question of who actually cooked this food. Issue 84 was the current one in August 2026, and the subscription delivers inside Turkey only, so a copy is something to carry home.
v-yemek.why: Read it for the recipes nobody else has written down: seven forgotten ones every issue, from Musa Dağdeviren.
facts: Quarterly print journal of food history and folk recipes, since January 2005
In print; annual subscription delivers inside Turkey only; Instagram @yemekvekulturdergisi_ciya

v-milor.name: Vedat Milor
v-milor.teaser: A Berkeley sociologist who became the country's most argued-with palate
v-milor.story: Born in 1955, Vedat Milor went through Galatasaray Lisesi, read economics at Boğaziçi, took a master's at the LSE and a doctorate in sociology at Berkeley, where his thesis was named the best of 1990 by the American Sociological Association. He then turned that apparatus on restaurants, first in the newspaper Milliyet and then in a long-running programme on NTV, and he now edits the English-language Gastromondiale. In Istanbul his verdict moves a booking sheet the way a star does, which is reason enough to know what he has said about a room before you sit down in it.
v-milor.why: Check his take before a big booking: a Milor verdict changes who can get a table.
facts: Restaurant critic and broadcaster; editor of Gastromondiale
Gastromondiale in English; his television work and social feeds in Turkish

v-oney.name: Aylin Öney Tan
v-oney.teaser: The one Turkish food writer still filing a weekly column in English
v-oney.story: Trained as an architect and once project manager on the World Bank's cultural heritage project in Turkey, Aylin Öney Tan writes on food for Hürriyet Daily News, the country's oldest English-language daily, and in Turkish for Cumhuriyet. The column is current rather than archival: she was filing through July 2026, on gastronomic diplomacy at state dinners, on the Culture Route Festival mapping fifty taste stops across Bursa, and on the seasonal logic Istanbul kitchens actually work to. For anyone without Turkish, it is the best way into Anatolian regional food, written by someone who has eaten her way across it.
v-oney.why: Read a month of her columns before you arrive and you will know what is in season when you land.
facts: Weekly food column in Hürriyet Daily News
English; her Cumhuriyet column is in Turkish

v-cb.name: Culinary Backstreets
v-cb.teaser: Two men in Istanbul writing up lunch, and they never lost the habit
v-cb.story: It began as Istanbul Eats, a blog run by Ansel Mullins, who worked in historic restoration, and Yigal Schleifer, then the Christian Science Monitor's Istanbul correspondent; the site first shows up in the web archive in April 2009. It has since grown into food tours and reporting across close to thirty cities, but Istanbul is still the deepest desk, with a city guide, regular dispatches and walking tours, and the old istanbuleats.com address now simply redirects here. The writing is about who cooks, where they came from and what the lunch counter down the street is doing this year.
v-cb.why: Search its Istanbul archive by neighbourhood before you walk one; the lunch counters it lists are the ones locals use.
facts: Food reporting, city guides and walking tours, with Istanbul as its deepest desk

v-cornucopia.name: Cornucopia
v-cornucopia.teaser: For people who came for the food and stayed for the Ottoman archive
v-cornucopia.story: Launched in 1992 and made between Scotland, London and Turkey, Cornucopia publishes two issues a year at a circulation above twenty thousand, edited by John Scott with Berrin Torolsan as publishing director. Its register is connoisseurial: architecture, textiles, gardens, Anatolian archaeology, and food treated as material culture rather than as a booking problem. A piece on a palace kitchen or a Bosphorus yalı will tell you more about what was eaten there than any menu. The complete digital archive of every issue comes with a subscription of about nineteen pounds a year, which is the real reason to sign up.
v-cornucopia.why: Buy the digital archive and search it for the place you are about to see.
facts: Biannual magazine on Turkish art, architecture, history and food, since 1992
cornucopia.net; print and digital; digital subscription about GBP 19 a year (seen Aug 2026)

v-recap.name: Turkey recap
v-recap.teaser: Why the bar you loved is suddenly not serving alcohol
v-recap.story: Turkey recap started as an English-language newsletter in October 2019, written by journalists based in Istanbul and Ankara; Diego Cupolo co-founded it with Raziye Akkoç. It is independent and reader-supported, published since 2023 by Kolektif Medya Derneği, an Istanbul non-profit, with one weekly letter on politics and foreign affairs and another on business and the economy, plus a Turkish-language strand. It is not a food publication, but licensing, alcohol regulation, inflation and the lira set what an Istanbul evening costs and whether the meyhane down the road can still pour, and this is where those changes get explained first.
v-recap.why: Subscribe for the month you are in the city: it explains the price and licensing shifts before the bill does.
facts: Independent news newsletter on Turkish politics and economy, two letters a week
turkeyrecap.com; paid, with a free trial

sources.label: GFMD: Turkey recap / Kolektif Medya Derneği

v-ohp.name: Ottoman History Podcast
v-ohp.teaser: Academics talking properly, without the academic gate
v-ohp.story: It started in March 2011 as an experiment in accessible scholarly production and became one of the largest digital resources of its kind on the Ottoman Empire and the modern Middle East. Chris Gratien, now at the University of Virginia, has recorded more than two hundred interviews with historians, and the project carries no advertising and takes no revenue. A parallel Turkish-language strand runs alongside the English one. For a cook or a guest heading for Istanbul, the archive has whole episodes on coffee, wine, famine and the millet system, each one a better primer than a guidebook chapter.
v-ohp.why: Search the archive for coffee and wine before the trip; the episodes change what you notice in the Spice Bazaar.
facts: Free scholarly podcast on Ottoman and modern Middle Eastern history, since March 2011
ottomanhistorypodcast.com, with a full episode guide; on Apple Podcasts and Spotify

v-iksv.name: İKSV — Istanbul Foundation for Culture and Arts
v-iksv.teaser: One foundation programmes most of the big weeks in the Istanbul year
v-iksv.story: İKSV runs the Istanbul Film Festival, the Music Festival, the Jazz Festival, the Theatre Festival, the Istanbul Biennial and the Design Biennial, plus Filmekimi and the year-round Salon İKSV stage, and it curates the Turkish Pavilion at the Venice Biennale. That makes its calendar the single page that tells you which week the city's halls, hotels and best tables will be full of festival crowds. Check it against your dates before you fix a dinner: a jazz night or a biennial opening may be worth moving a booking for, and a sold-out week is worth knowing about early.
v-iksv.why: Check the calendar against your dates before you book a single table.
facts: The foundation behind Istanbul's film, music, jazz and theatre festivals and the Biennial
iksv.org; calendar and free e-bülten sign-up

v-timeout.name: Time Out Istanbul
v-timeout.teaser: The English backstop when you need something open tonight
v-timeout.story: Time Out runs a full local Istanbul edition in English and in Turkish, across restaurants and cafes, things to do, film, music and nightlife, art and culture. It is a commercial listings operation, not a critical guide, and it should never settle an argument about where to eat. Where it earns its place is the practical layer: opening hours, one-off events and whatever has just opened in the street you are standing in. Its listings are often the only English record of a shop's hours, though many are undated, so treat a time there as a lead to confirm rather than a promise.

_notes: Couldn't confirm with a dated 2026 source: Turkey recap, Yemek ve Kültür (issue 84, Aug 2026) and Aylin Öney Tan's column (filing through July 2026). The old card's August claims are kept; recheck them before publishing. Salı Pazarı: Friday as a second day comes from CNN Türk (report undated) and an aggregator; confirm the week locally. Vefa season is not stated anywhere for 2026; October–April is the old card's guidance. Turkey recap: the old card's Turkish-edition domain 'studyorecap.com' could not be confirmed (search shows a turkeyrecapturkce Substack), so it was dropped.
